gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive study that develops corpus poisoning and a novel backdoor attack on the dense retriever during fine-tuning, with the goal of maximizing Attack Success Rate (ASR) for goals like malicious link injection and denial of service. Paper B is a defensive study that inverts training-free prompt injection attack methods to build a defense that operates at the prompt/generation level, with the goal of minimizing ASR against existing attacks. The action_policy is opposite (attack vs. defense), the intervention_point differs (retriever fine-tuning vs. inference-time prompt manipulation), the failure_type differs (retrieval-stage poisoning susceptibility vs. generator inability to ignore injected instructions), and although both report ASR, the optimization direction is inverted, so the metric_target is not commensurable. Evidence_assumption also diverges: Paper A presumes attacker control over corpus or training data, Paper B presumes a deployed LLM facing standard injection attempts in retrieved content.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to either (a) attack the same RAG configuration under a shared threat model and report ASR in the same direction, or (b) evaluate Paper B's defense against Paper A's specific retriever-poisoning/backdoor attacks on a shared benchmark, with matched LLMs, retrievers, corpora, and injection payloads, so that lower ASR for the defended system can be directly contrasted with the undefended ASR achieved by the attack.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper is trying to make a number go up because that number represents an adversary winning, while the other paper is trying to make essentially the same number go down because the same outcome means the system was compromised. They also touch different parts of the retrieval-augmented pipeline and operate under different threat scenarios. Putting their headline numbers next to each other on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about relative strength that the underlying studies do not support.

gold_rationale: Paper A (ADMIT) proposes an offensive technique: a few-shot semantic knowledge poisoning attack on RAG-based fact-checking, reporting Attack Success Rate (ASR ~86%) across 4 retrievers, 11 LLMs, and 4 fact-checking benchmarks, assuming credible evidence dominates the pool. Paper B (OpenRAG-Soc) is a benchmark/harness for social-web indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning, with web-native carriers (HTML/Markdown/Unicode), packaged with deployable defenses, and reports a multi-dimensional set of outcomes (answer-time attack rate, rank shifts in sparse/dense retrievers, utility, latency). The threat models (semantic claim-flipping vs. carrier-based IPI), domains (fact-checking vs. social-web QA), measurement schemes, and roles (single attack proposal vs. benchmark+defense suite) all diverge, so the two main results do not occupy a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to be instantiated on the same corpus and threat model (e.g., the same social-web or fact-checking dataset), with the same primary outcome (e.g., end-to-end attack success at answer time under matched retriever/LLM configurations) and matched poisoning budgets/carrier formats. Running ADMIT inside the OpenRAG-Soc harness, or replicating OpenRAG-Soc carrier attacks on the fact-checking benchmarks ADMIT uses, with identical retrievers, generators, and defense settings, would be required before any side-by-side ranking is meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle different threat scenarios on different corpora with different scoring schemes and different goals: one introduces a new poisoning technique against fact-checking RAG and reports a single success-rate headline, while the other delivers a benchmark plus defenses for social-web indirect prompt injection and reports ranking shifts, utility, and latency. A practitioner placing the headline numbers next to each other on one chart would draw conclusions about relative severity or robustness that the underlying setups do not support.

gold_rationale: Both papers target the same threat model (corpus poisoning of dense-retriever RAG) and both propose retriever-side defenses, so the failure_type and broad intervention_point align. However, the action_policy differs substantively: Paper A is a reranking/score-suppression mechanism that preserves passages but reorders them using probe-gradient instability signals, whereas Paper B is a binary detection mechanism that flags poisoned documents. Their metric_target also diverges — Paper A reports robustness–utility trade-offs, poisoned Top-K exposure, and end-to-end attack success across three datasets and three backbones, while Paper B reports detection rates centered on a medical Q&A universal-poisoning setting (with 225 setup combinations). The evidence_assumption is narrower in B (universal poisoning, medical/PII focus) than in A (multiple attack families including trigger-based and misleading-evidence). Side-by-side comparability exists at a high level but the headline numbers do not measure the same quantity on the same workloads.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation harness with: (1) the same corpora, retrievers, and attack implementations covering both papers' threat models; (2) a common metric set that captures both detection performance (precision/recall on poisoned passages) and downstream impact (poisoned Top-K rate, attack success rate, clean-task utility); (3) treating Paper B's detector as a filter feeding Paper A's reranker (or vice versa) so each can be evaluated as a pipeline stage; (4) matched adaptive-attack protocols; and (5) reporting on at least one common domain such as medical Q&A so the domain-specific claims in B and the general claims in A overlap.
independent_rubric_rationale: A reader scanning a single leaderboard would see one paper reporting how well poisoned passages are flagged in a medical Q&A setting and another reporting reordering quality and downstream answer corruption across several general benchmarks. Because the headline numbers describe different outputs (flag-or-not vs reorder-and-keep) on different corpora, ranking them by a single column would create a false impression of head-to-head superiority, even though both target the same underlying threat and could plausibly be combined.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a defense paper proposing InstructDetector to detect indirect prompt injection (IPI) in standard text-based RAG via hidden-state/gradient features, reporting detection accuracy (99.60% in-domain, 96.90% OOD) and ASR reduction (0.03%) on BIPIA. Paper B is an offense paper proposing two knowledge poisoning attacks (TKPA, UKPA) against GraphRAG by altering a few words in source text used for graph construction, reporting attack success rate (93.1%) and QA accuracy collapse (95%→50%). All five coordinates diverge: (1) failure_type differs (instruction injection in retrieved docs vs. corrupting graph construction); (2) evidence_assumption differs (adversary plants instructions at inference-time retrieval vs. adversary edits source corpus before graph build); (3) intervention_point differs (LLM-side detector vs. source-text manipulation in graph extraction pipeline); (4) metric_target differs (detection accuracy / ASR reduction on BIPIA vs. attack success / QA degradation on graph QA); (5) action_policy differs (filter suspicious documents vs. craft poisoned narratives). The papers also play opposite roles (defender vs. attacker) on different system variants (RAG vs. GraphRAG).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to address the same threat surface (e.g., both attacks on GraphRAG or both defenses against IPI), share the same target system (text-RAG or GraphRAG), use a common benchmark and threat model, and report comparable quantities (e.g., both ASR under matched attack conditions, or both detection performance against matched poisoning attacks). At minimum a shared dataset and a shared role (attack-vs-attack or defense-vs-defense) is required.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works sit on opposite sides of the security problem and on different system architectures: one is a protective tool that screens retrieved text in conventional RAG, while the other is an offensive technique that corrupts the graph built by GraphRAG by editing source documents. Their headline numbers measure different things (how well malicious snippets are caught vs. how reliably the adversary can flip answers) on different benchmarks. A practitioner who saw them side by side on a single ranked list could easily conflate a defender's success rate with an attacker's success rate, or assume the GraphRAG attack is relevant to the text-RAG defender's setting, leading to seriously wrong conclusions about which system is safer or stronger.

gold_rationale: Paper A proposes DTR, a training-free RAG method that uses generation uncertainty to gate retrieval and a dual-path retrieval mechanism, evaluated on five open-domain QA benchmarks with EM and F1 against standard RAG baselines. Paper B presents knowornot, a library/methodology for evaluating out-of-knowledge-base (OOKB) robustness — i.e., whether LLMs abstain on queries outside the knowledge base — and demonstrates it via the PolicyBench benchmark. The failure_type differs (retrieval noise / sparse query handling vs. hallucination on OOKB queries / abstention behavior). The intervention_point differs (a new RAG pipeline vs. an evaluation framework/library). The metric_target differs (EM/F1 on open-domain QA vs. OOKB robustness / abstention rates on domain-specific QA chatbots). The action_policy differs (adaptive retrieval triggering and evidence selection vs. systematic synthetic-question generation and judging pipeline). The evidence_assumption also diverges (general open-domain corpora vs. closed domain-specific knowledge bases with explicit out-of-scope partitions). No shared dataset, baseline, or scoring scheme overlaps.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require both works to target the same problem on a shared benchmark with comparable scoring — for example, running DTR's selective-retrieval pipeline through knowornot's OOKB evaluation on PolicyBench (measuring abstention behavior), or, conversely, having Paper B report EM/F1 on the same open-domain QA datasets DTR uses. At minimum, an overlapping benchmark, identical generator models, and a common evaluation protocol (either QA accuracy or abstention/OOKB robustness scored the same way) would be needed before placing results side-by-side.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers tackle fundamentally different problems with non-overlapping evaluation regimes. Paper A reports exact-match and F1 gains on open-domain QA from a new adaptive RAG pipeline, while Paper B contributes an evaluation library and a policy-domain benchmark focused on whether models correctly decline to answer when the knowledge base lacks support. A practitioner viewing these headline numbers on one leaderboard would conflate accuracy improvements on standard QA with abstention/robustness behavior on out-of-scope queries, drawing conclusions neither paper supports.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic/benchmark study of over-searching: it characterizes when search-augmented LLMs invoke retrieval unnecessarily (including on unanswerable queries), introduces Tokens Per Correctness (TPC) as a cost-efficiency metric, releases OverSearchQA, and stresses abstention behavior. Paper B is a method paper for dynamic RAG that triggers retrieval based on pre-training corpus statistics (entity frequency and co-occurrence via Infini-gram), reporting EM gains of 5–12 points on multi-hop QA with OLMo-2, Llama-3, Qwen2.5, GPT-4.1/5. The two operate on different problems (suppress unnecessary searches and improve abstention vs. trigger retrieval to reduce hallucination), use disjoint benchmarks (OverSearchQA vs. multi-hop/biomedical QA), and report different headline numbers (TPC and abstention vs. EM). Their action policies (abstain/search vs. retrieve/not retrieve based on corpus signal) and intervention designs (analysis + lightweight mitigation vs. novel trigger method) diverge. The evidence_assumption axis is partially shared (both touch retrieval-time signals) but used to different ends.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A direct comparison would need (1) a shared evaluation suite that mixes answerable and unanswerable queries, (2) joint reporting of both a cost-efficiency score (e.g., TPC or search-call rate) and an accuracy/EM score, (3) the same backbone models and retriever, and (4) a unified policy space (when-to-retrieve and when-to-abstain) so each system's trigger logic is evaluated on identical inputs. Without these, TPC/abstention numbers from A and EM-gain numbers from B cannot be placed on one axis.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works target different problems within retrieval-augmented LLMs. Paper A studies when systems call the search tool too often, including on questions that have no answer, and scores systems with a cost-per-correct-answer style score plus abstention behavior on its own benchmark. Paper B proposes a corpus-statistics trigger for dynamic retrieval and reports exact-match improvements on multi-hop and biomedical QA with a different model lineup. The benchmarks, headline numbers, and goals (cut wasteful searches and refuse unknowable questions vs. lift answer correctness on answerable multi-hop questions) do not align, so putting A's TPC/abstention results next to B's EM gains on one leaderboard would suggest the two are competing on the same task when they are not, leading a practitioner to draw unwarranted conclusions about which approach is 'better.'

gold_rationale: Paper A snippet is unavailable, but its title clearly scopes the work to Knowledge-Graph RAG with a causality-aware calibration framework for deciding when to trust retrieved KG facts. Paper B targets generic text RAG and uses reinforcement learning with a multi-stage gated reward to jointly train grounded answering and abstention, with data constructed from heterogeneous retrievers. The evidence_assumption differs (structured KG triples vs unstructured retrieved passages from heterogeneous retrievers). The intervention_point differs (post-hoc/inference-time calibration vs RL fine-tuning of the generator). The metric_target differs (calibration/trust accuracy on KG-RAG vs overall accuracy plus answer-vs-abstain balance on QA benchmarks B reports). The action_policy differs (trust/no-trust gating over KG-derived answers vs evidence-extraction-then-answer-or-IDK). Even granting that both touch the 'reliability of RAG' theme, the underlying tasks, training regimes, and likely benchmark suites do not line up.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Shared retrieval substrate (both KG-RAG or both passage-RAG, or an explicit cross-modality protocol), evaluation on a common benchmark suite with identical splits, a shared definition and metric for abstention/trust (e.g., selective accuracy, coverage-risk curves, calibration error), and matched base LLMs and inference budgets. Without aligning these, headline numbers from each paper measure different constructs.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems operate over different kinds of retrieved knowledge (a structured graph versus general retrieved passages) and are trained or adjusted in very different ways, so their reported headline numbers almost certainly come from different test suites and reflect different notions of 'reliability.' A practitioner skimming a combined leaderboard would likely draw an unwarranted ordering between them and pick the wrong tool for their deployment setting.

gold_rationale: Paper A provides only a title ('Reliable Decision-Making via Calibration-Oriented Retrieval-Augmented Generation') with no text snippet available. While the title suggests a calibration-focused RAG approach that might thematically overlap with Paper B's selective generation / abstention framework, none of the five coordinates can be verified for Paper A: the targeted error mode, the framing of retrieved evidence, where in the pipeline the change is made, the headline numeric target, and the downstream policy (e.g., abstain vs. answer) are all unknown. Paper B is well-specified: it introduces a sufficient-context classifier, evaluates Gemini/GPT/Claude/Mistral/Gemma on QA datasets, and reports a 2–10% improvement in the fraction of correct answers among responded queries via a guided-abstention selective generation method. Without Paper A's details, a principled judgment of comparability cannot be reached, so a conservative 'underspecified' verdict is warranted.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Access to Paper A's abstract/method section to identify: (1) the specific reliability failure being addressed (miscalibration vs. hallucination vs. over-answering), (2) the assumed role of retrieved evidence (sufficiency, relevance, calibration signal), (3) where the change is applied (retriever, generator, post-hoc selector), (4) the headline metric and dataset (e.g., ECE, selective accuracy, coverage-risk, answer correctness on Natural Questions/HotpotQA), and (5) the downstream behavior (abstention, confidence thresholding, re-retrieval). Both papers would also need shared base models, datasets, and an aligned operating point (e.g., matched coverage) to be placed on one leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: With only a title from Paper A, there is no way to know what numbers, datasets, base models, or evaluation protocol it reports. A practitioner could be misled or could be fine — there simply is not enough information from one side of the pair to decide.

gold_rationale: Although both papers use the word 'distractor', they address fundamentally different phenomena. Paper A (PrismRAG) targets semi-relevant retrieved passages that degrade factual QA, measures factuality on 12 RAG QA benchmarks, and intervenes via supervised fine-tuning on distractor-mixed QA pairs plus reasoning training, reporting +5.4% factuality. Paper B (DistractionIF) targets instruction-like text embedded in reference material that hijacks the model into treating data as commands, measures instruction-following robustness on a custom DistractionIF benchmark, intervenes via GRPO reinforcement learning, and reports +15.5% robustness. All five coordinates differ — the threat model (semantic relevance noise vs. instruction injection from benign text), the benchmark family, the training paradigm, the evaluated quantity, and the desired model behavior (synthesize accurate answers vs. ignore embedded directives) are not aligned. The shared vocabulary creates a superficial impression of overlap that does not survive inspection.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both systems to be evaluated on the same benchmark with the same notion of 'distractor' (either semi-relevant retrieval noise or instruction-like noise in reference text), using a common scoring rubric (factuality vs. instruction-following robustness), and ideally with matched base models and training compute. At minimum, one would need to run PrismRAG on DistractionIF and the GRPO-trained model on the 12 RAG QA benchmarks to produce comparable numbers under each threat model separately.
independent_rubric_rationale: Although both works share the word 'distractor' in their titles, they study two distinct problems: one is about confusing semi-relevant passages degrading factual answers in retrieval QA, while the other is about instruction-like phrases inside reference documents being mistakenly executed as commands. The headline numbers 5.4% and 15.5% are computed on different benchmarks, with different scoring rubrics, and against different threat models. A practitioner skimming a single leaderboard with these two entries would likely conclude one method dominates the other, when in reality they solve disjoint problems and neither has been shown to help with the other's setting.

gold_rationale: Paper A (KV Fusion) targets positional bias ('Lost in the Middle') in decoder-only generators by altering KV-cache prefill so that order of retrieved passages does not affect output; its headline metrics are position invariance and accuracy on NQ/TriviaQA/POPQA under shuffled passage order. Paper B (LDAR) targets distractor interference and the RAG-vs-long-context trade-off by training an adaptive retriever that selects a variable number of passages; its headline metric is the performance/token-usage Pareto curve over six knowledge-intensive benchmarks across multiple LLM backbones (including GPT-4o). The pipeline stage being modified differs (generator-side cache fusion vs. retriever-side selection policy), the headline failure mode differs (order sensitivity vs. distractor amplification under large contexts), and the reported quantities are not on a common axis. Datasets overlap only loosely, and neither paper's numbers are reported under conditions that the other's framework controls for.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation suite with overlapping LLM backbones and identical retriever/candidate pool, reporting (a) accuracy under shuffled vs. canonical passage order at matched k and token budgets, and (b) accuracy vs. token-usage Pareto curves. Ideally one would also run a combined system (LDAR retriever feeding into a KV-Fusion generator) to disentangle retriever-side and generator-side contributions, and report variance across at least the union of NQ/TriviaQA/POPQA and the six LDAR benchmarks under one prompting protocol.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems modify different parts of the RAG pipeline and report headline numbers on largely different benchmarks with different LLM backbones, different passage-count regimes, and different evaluation emphases (robustness to context ordering versus a performance-vs-token-cost curve). Dropping their top-line scores into a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to infer a head-to-head ranking that the underlying experiments do not actually support, and could obscure the fact that the two approaches are largely complementary rather than substitutable.

gold_rationale: Paper A proposes a training-free decoding-time technique (entropy-based document-parallel ensemble plus contrastive decoding across layers) evaluated on open-domain QA. Paper B proposes a training-time recipe (supervised fine-tuning with distractor documents plus chain-of-thought rationales) evaluated on domain-specific corpora (PubMed, HotpotQA, Gorilla). Although both target distraction/noise in RAG (shared failure framing), they differ on the intervention point (decoding vs. fine-tuning), the resource and data assumptions (no training data vs. domain training set with distractors), the action policy (probability reweighting vs. parameter update with rationales), and the evaluation regime (general open-domain QA vs. specialized in-domain RAG). These are largely complementary rather than competing methods and cannot be ranked directly from headline numbers.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared base LLM and retriever, a common set of benchmarks (e.g., both evaluated on the same open-domain and domain-specific splits with identical retrieved contexts), matched compute/data budgets, explicit reporting of training vs. training-free regime so practitioners see the cost trade-off, and ideally an ablation that combines the two (RAFT-tuned model with entropy decoding) to show whether the gains are additive or overlapping. Without this, the two numbers belong on separate leaderboards.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers solve adjacent but structurally different problems with very different recipes. One simply re-weights output probabilities at generation time without touching model weights, while the other rewrites the model itself through supervised tuning on domain examples that include irrelevant passages and reasoning traces. They also report results on different benchmark families - broad open-domain question answering versus specialized domains like PubMed and Gorilla. Placing their headline scores side-by-side on a single leaderboard would hide these differences in setup, compute cost, data requirements, and target conditions, so a practitioner choosing between them based on the numbers alone would likely make a poor choice.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic empirical audit of context utilization across model scale (360M–8B), with no proposed method, using an oracle retrieval condition to isolate utilization from retrieval quality. Paper B proposes a new architectural method (END) that uses a linear prober on early LLM layers to drop noisy context chunks, primarily targeting general (often larger) LLMs in noisy long-context settings. The five coordinates diverge: (1) failure_type — A frames the problem as scale-specific utilization deficit; B frames it as generic noise distraction; (2) evidence_assumption — A includes an oracle clean-context regime to isolate behavior; B assumes mixed informative/noisy chunks; (3) intervention_point — A performs no model or pipeline modification; B inserts an early-layer chunk-dropping module; (4) metric_target — A reports extraction accuracy, parametric-knowledge retention, and error-mode breakdowns; B reports task accuracy and computational efficiency gains; (5) action_policy — A concludes RAG yields a net-negative trade-off at sub-7B scale; B recommends adopting END to improve performance and efficiency. The studies answer different questions on different model regimes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both works to share a common evaluation: (a) the same model-size ladder (including sub-7B models that Paper A studies and any larger models END is tuned on), (b) overlapping retrieval/noise conditions (oracle clean passages plus noisy passages), (c) common outcome measures (e.g., accuracy on parametric-known vs. parametric-unknown questions, plus efficiency), and (d) a clear ablation showing whether END changes the utilization bottleneck Paper A identifies. Without such a shared protocol, a numeric or ranked comparison is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper is a diagnostic study concluding that small (≤7B) models largely cannot exploit retrieved passages, even when the answer is provably present. The other introduces an early-layer chunk-dropping technique for LLMs in noisy contexts and reports accuracy and efficiency gains, mostly outside the small-model regime. Putting these two headline numbers on a single leaderboard would let a practitioner read a pessimistic scale-limited diagnosis and an optimistic engineering result as if they spoke to the same question, and would obscure that the two are evaluated under different model sizes, different context regimes, and different reporting conventions.

gold_rationale: Snippets are unavailable, so judgment relies on titles and known scope. MIRAGE positions itself as a metric-intensive benchmark, i.e., a curated dataset plus a battery of scoring protocols for RAG systems. RAGAs positions itself as an automated, largely reference-free framework (typically LLM-judge based) for scoring RAG outputs along faithfulness/relevance/etc. These occupy different layers of the evaluation stack: one supplies the testbed, the other supplies the scorer. They are complementary, not substitutable, so any direct ranking would conflate distinct contributions. The break is primarily at the intervention_point (benchmark artifact vs. scoring methodology), the metric_target (benchmark numbers on RAG systems vs. correlation/agreement of an automatic judge with human ratings), and the action_policy (use this benchmark to grade your RAG pipeline vs. use this judge to grade RAG outputs anywhere).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) both works evaluated as automatic judges on a common meta-evaluation set with matched correlation statistics against the same human references, or (b) both works evaluated as benchmarks using identical RAG systems, retrieval corpora, prompts, and metric implementations. At minimum, a shared protocol specifying dataset, models under test, and metric definitions is needed before any leaderboard placement.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works play different roles in the RAG evaluation pipeline: one supplies a scored test suite for grading RAG systems, while the other supplies an automatic scorer that can grade arbitrary RAG outputs. Putting their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would imply they are competing solutions to the same problem, which would steer a practitioner toward a false either-or choice. Confidence is tempered because no snippets were provided, but the titles make the role mismatch reasonably clear.

gold_rationale: Paper A (ReEval) targets hallucination in RAG generation, using transferable adversarial perturbations of retrieved evidence to elicit and measure hallucinated outputs. Paper B (UDCG) targets misalignment of classical IR ranking metrics (nDCG/MAP/MRR) with LLM consumption of retrieved passages, proposing a utility- and distraction-aware cumulative gain that correlates better with end-to-end answer accuracy. The failure mode being diagnosed differs (generation hallucination vs. retrieval-metric–LLM misalignment), the intervention point differs (perturb evidence to stress-test generator vs. redesign ranking metric for retriever evaluation), the headline metric differs (hallucination/robustness rates vs. correlation between ranking metric and answer accuracy), and the operational policy differs (produce adversarial test items vs. score rankings with a new gain function). Only the evidence_assumption partially overlaps in that both presume retrieved passages condition LLM output, but they exploit this assumption in incompatible ways.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task and outcome would be needed, e.g., both methods evaluated as predictors of the same downstream RAG answer quality on the same datasets and LLMs, or both used to score the same retriever/generator pipeline on a common hallucination or accuracy benchmark with matched evidence sets and held-out splits. Without alignment on what is being measured and which stage of the pipeline is being scored, single-leaderboard placement is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers address substantively different questions about retrieval-augmented systems. One probes how easily a generator can be pushed into producing wrong content when its supporting passages are adversarially altered; the other proposes a new way to score ranked lists of passages so the score tracks downstream answer correctness. Their headline numbers live in different units and answer different practitioner questions, so juxtaposing them on a single leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head contest that does not exist and would likely cause a reader to draw conclusions neither paper supports.

gold_rationale: Paper A (MTRAG-UN) is a benchmark/dataset contribution comprising 666 multi-turn RAG tasks across 6 domains targeting unanswerable, underspecified, non-standalone questions and unclear responses. Paper B (RAGLAB) is, per its title, a modular research framework/toolkit for RAG. These are categorically different artifact types: one defines evaluation tasks for a narrow conversational challenge space, the other provides infrastructure for implementing and running RAG pipelines. The diagnosed problem, the proposed remedy, the kind of evidence reported, the quantitative target, and the downstream practitioner uptake all diverge. Paper B's text snippet is unavailable, which lowers confidence slightly, but the title and venue (EMNLP demo) strongly signal a tools paper, not a head-to-head competitor of a benchmark.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to make claims about the same outcome on overlapping settings, e.g., both reporting RAG system scores on a shared multi-turn benchmark, or both proposing benchmarks intended to measure the same conversational phenomena, with shared evaluation protocols and at least one common system or metric. As framed, the only honest combined use is complementary (run RAGLAB-implemented systems on MTRAG-UN tasks), not ranked comparison.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers deliver fundamentally different kinds of artifacts to the RAG community: one supplies a curated set of difficult multi-turn conversation tasks for stress-testing systems, while the other supplies a research toolkit/codebase for building and running RAG pipelines. Putting their headline numbers on a single leaderboard would tell a practitioner nothing useful, because the headline quantities answer different questions and the artifacts play complementary rather than rival roles.

gold_rationale: Paper A (SeedRG) targets benchmark contamination/knowledge leakage as the failure mode, assumes that valid RAG evaluation requires questions outside parametric memory, intervenes at the dataset-construction stage via reasoning-graph extraction plus type-constrained entity substitution, optimizes for leakage reduction (~78%) while preserving reasoning difficulty, and recommends using regenerated benchmarks. Paper B (Judge-as-a-Judge) targets evaluator unreliability of LLM judges as the failure mode, assumes judge-consistency is a reasonable proxy for evaluation quality, intervenes at the judging/scoring layer, optimizes for judge-consistency, and recommends a consistency-based judging procedure. All five coordinates diverge: the two works fix orthogonal bottlenecks in the RAG evaluation pipeline (data quality vs. evaluator quality) and report numbers on incompatible quantities. Even though both nominally aim at 'better RAG evaluation,' their headline results do not occupy the same axis and cannot be ranked head-to-head. Paper B's snippet is unavailable, which limits certainty, but the title is sufficiently specific to ground the divergence.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require both papers to (1) address the same bottleneck in RAG evaluation (either benchmark construction or judge scoring, not one each), (2) report results on a shared dataset and a shared evaluation protocol, and (3) optimize a common scoring quantity (e.g., both reporting leakage rates on the same seed benchmarks, or both reporting judge-human agreement on the same response set). Without that, only a complementary/stacked evaluation makes sense: apply SeedRG to build the test set, then apply Judge-Consistency to score outputs, and report separate diagnostic numbers for each layer rather than a single ranking.
independent_rubric_rationale: These two works approach RAG evaluation from very different angles. SeedRG rewrites benchmark questions so they can no longer be solved from a model's memorized knowledge, while Judge-as-a-Judge tries to make the LLM scorer itself more trustworthy by checking that its verdicts are self-consistent. Their headline numbers describe entirely different things — one is about how much memorization-shortcutting was removed from the test set, the other is about how stable or agreeable the scoring procedure is. Dropping both onto a single leaderboard and reading off 'who wins' would let a practitioner think one work supersedes the other, when in reality they fix complementary weaknesses in the evaluation pipeline.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic and debiasing study of source-credibility preferences under inter-context conflicts using synthetic sources, with primary numbers reported as source-preference scores and repetition-bias reduction percentages (e.g., up to 79.2% bias reduction while retaining 72.5% of preferences). Paper B is a pipeline (CARE-RAG) that combines parameter-aware evidence extraction, retrieved-evidence refinement, distilled conflict-driven summarization, and a QA Repair step, evaluated against RAG baselines on revised QA benchmarks with accuracy-style metrics. The targeted failure differs (source-credibility/repetition bias vs. internal/external knowledge conflict harming QA correctness), the evidence setup differs (synthetic source-annotated passages vs. real retrieval over QA corpora with internal model knowledge), the locus of change differs (fine-tuning the base LLM vs. an end-to-end multi-stage pipeline plus benchmark cleanup), the measurement differs (bias/preference metrics vs. QA accuracy), and the deployment story differs (preserve fair source treatment vs. produce trustworthy answers). None of the five coordinates align.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require the two systems to be evaluated on the same task with the same metric, e.g., either (a) measuring CARE-RAG's source-preference and repetition-bias profile on Paper A's synthetic source benchmark, or (b) measuring Paper A's fine-tuned debiased model as a drop-in generator inside a RAG pipeline on Paper B's revised QA datasets with QA accuracy reported under matched retrievers and conflict conditions. The two should also share the same underlying base LLMs and the same definition of 'conflict' (inter-context source conflict vs. internal-vs-external conflict) before any ranking is attempted.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two headline numbers describe fundamentally different things: one reports how much a debiasing procedure shifts a model's tendency to favor certain kinds of source labels while preserving prior preference patterns, while the other reports answer-correctness gains for a multi-stage RAG pipeline on cleaned question-answering benchmarks. Placing 79.2% bias reduction next to QA accuracy gains on a single leaderboard would suggest the systems are solving the same problem and competing on the same yardstick, which they are not, so a practitioner choosing between them based on such a ranking would draw seriously wrong conclusions about which is 'better' for their use case.

gold_rationale: Both papers target the same failure_type (LLM unfaithfulness to provided context under knowledge conflict in RAG-style settings) and share a similar action_policy goal (produce context-grounded answers). However, the intervention_point differs fundamentally: Paper A modifies model weights via DPO alignment using preference pairs of faithful vs. stubborn responses, while Paper B operates at inference-time by identifying fact-level conflicts and invoking a self-thinking reasoning process without weight updates. The evidence_assumption also likely differs: Paper A evaluates on its own ConFiQA benchmark (synthetically constructed knowledge-conflict QA), while Paper B's snippet refers to 'extensive experiments' and 'state-of-the-art' comparisons on unspecified (likely different) benchmarks. The metric_target framings differ as well: Paper A reports relative improvement percentages (35%-280%) on open-source models, whereas Paper B frames results as outperforming SOTA, with no shared headline metric visible in the snippet.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require (1) evaluating both methods on the same benchmark suite (e.g., ConFiQA plus the benchmarks used by Paper B), (2) using the same backbone LLMs and reporting identically-defined faithfulness metrics (e.g., memorization rate, faithfulness accuracy), (3) explicitly accounting for the training-time vs inference-time intervention asymmetry, including compute cost, applicability to closed-source models, and whether the DPO-aligned model is used as the backbone for the inference-time framework, and (4) controlling for differences in conflict construction (synthetic counterfactual vs naturally occurring retrieval conflicts).
independent_rubric_rationale: A practitioner browsing a single leaderboard with both headline numbers would get a partly misleading impression. The two systems address the same context-grounding problem in retrieval-augmented question answering, so a side-by-side ranking is tempting, but they operate at different stages of the pipeline (weight tuning versus inference-time reasoning) and appear to be measured on different test sets with different score definitions. Without harmonized backbones, datasets, and scoring, any direct ranking would conflate genuine quality differences with setup differences and would hide the practical trade-offs (cost of preference data and tuning vs added latency from explicit reasoning steps) that determine which approach is preferable in deployment.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a position paper arguing that retrieval-augmented systems pose communication and safety risks in medical settings; its failure_type concerns pragmatic/clinical communication harm, its evidence_assumption is argumentative-normative drawing on prior literature, its intervention_point is system design and deployment policy for medical RAG, its metric_target is qualitative safety/communicative adequacy, and its action_policy is high-level recommendations to developers and clinicians. Paper B is an empirical benchmarking study of how decoder LLMs use information located at different positions within long contexts; its failure_type is position-dependent utilization (U-shaped curve), evidence_assumption is controlled multi-document QA and key-value retrieval experiments, intervention_point is context construction/document ordering, metric_target is task accuracy as a function of input position and length, and action_policy is prompt/context engineering guidance. All five coordinates diverge, so no shared yardstick exists for ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation setting would be needed, e.g., both papers measuring the same outcome (such as factual accuracy or safety-of-response) on the same medical-RAG benchmark under matched retrieval and context conditions, with comparable quantitative scores and aligned definitions of what counts as success or harm.
independent_rubric_rationale: Paper A is a normative position piece warning about safety risks of retrieval-augmented systems used to communicate medical information to patients, while Paper B is a controlled empirical study quantifying how decoder language models utilize information placed at different positions within long context windows on QA and key-value tasks. The two works ask different questions, produce different kinds of outputs (recommendations vs. accuracy curves), and target different user concerns. Placing their headline results side by side on one leaderboard would seriously mislead a practitioner because the numbers and claims are not commensurable and pertain to unrelated phenomena.

gold_rationale: The two papers target different failure_types: Paper A (KnowPO) addresses conflict between an LLM's internal parametric knowledge and the external retrieved passage, plus contextual ignorance/overinclusion behaviors, while Paper B addresses inter-document conflict where supposedly relevant retrieved documents contain counterfactual or fabricated content. Their evidence_assumptions differ: KnowPO builds a constructed preference dataset spanning error types, whereas Paper B introduces MACNOISE, a machine-generated counterfactual-noise corpus. The intervention_points diverge as well: KnowPO modifies the generator via DPO-style preference training, while Paper B either trains a separate discriminator or uses GPT-3.5 prompting to filter conflicting documents. The action_policies also differ: KnowPO promotes adaptive selection (adhere to retrieval when relevant, fall back when not), whereas Paper B emphasizes discerning/discarding counterfactual documents before answering. Metric targets overlap only loosely (QA-style accuracy), but on different benchmarks and conflict definitions, so the headline '37% improvement' in A is not commensurable with B's robustness gains.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A fair comparison would require both methods to be evaluated on a shared benchmark that contains (i) parametric-vs-retrieved conflicts and (ii) inter-document counterfactual noise, using identical retrievers, base LLMs, and prompt templates, with matched metrics (e.g., exact-match/F1 under controlled noise ratios) and baselines. Ideally KnowPO's preference-tuned generator and Paper B's discriminator/prompting pipeline would be tested both in isolation and stacked, so the contributions of generator-side training and document-side filtering can be disentangled.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing these two systems side by side on a single leaderboard would give practitioners the wrong impression. One paper tackles the tension between what the model already 'knows' and what a passage says, while the other tackles the situation where several retrieved passages disagree with each other because some are fabricated. They use different datasets, different base models, and different pipeline components (generator preference tuning versus a separate discriminator or GPT-3.5 prompting), so a headline number from one cannot be read as better or worse than the other without substantial caveats.

gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets available), Paper A targets hierarchical planning for complex multi-step tasks, combining KG-RAG with symbolic verification of generated plans. Paper B targets knowledge gaps in graph foundation models via graph-structured retrieval. The failure types differ (invalid/incomplete plans vs. missing graph-domain knowledge in GFMs), the intervention points differ (planner pipeline with verifier vs. GFM training/inference loop), the metric targets differ (plan validity / task completion vs. graph learning benchmarks such as node/link/graph-level tasks), and the action policies differ (emitting executable hierarchical plans vs. emitting graph predictions). The only shared trait is the broad evidence stance that graph-structured retrieval supplies useful context, which is too generic to support a head-to-head ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on a shared benchmark with a shared task definition and identical scoring (e.g., both run on the same planning suite, or both run on the same GFM benchmark suite), with matched input/output formats and matched retrieval corpora. Absent that, any combined leaderboard would be conflating two different research problems.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works operate in different problem spaces: one produces executable multi-step plans that are checked symbolically, while the other strengthens general-purpose graph learning models with graph-based retrieval. Their reported scores would come from non-overlapping benchmarks and incompatible scoring schemes, so dropping them into a single ranking would push a practitioner toward conclusions the underlying numbers do not support.

gold_rationale: Based on titles and venues (no snippets supplied), the two works target disjoint problem settings. Paper A addresses outside-knowledge Visual Question Answering, where the input is an image plus question and the system retrieves textual passages using entity-focused dense retrieval; the failure mode is poor passage recall when visual entities are not well represented in DPR encodings, evidence is multimodal (image + Wikipedia-scale corpus), the intervention point is the retriever, the metric target is OK-VQA-style answer accuracy plus retrieval recall, and the action policy is an entity-aware dense retriever. Paper B addresses closed-domain legal/insurance QA over Quebec automobile insurance documents using RAG; the failure mode is hallucination or unfaithful generation in a regulated narrow domain, evidence is text-only domain corpora, the intervention point spans retrieval + generation, the metric target is generation quality on insurance questions, and the action policy is a domain-specific RAG pipeline. All five coordinates differ, so the two headline results cannot be placed on a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require either (a) both systems being evaluated on the same QA benchmark with identical inputs, corpora, and scoring, or (b) reframing the comparison narrowly around a shared methodological claim (e.g., entity-aware retrieval techniques vs. domain-adapted retrieval) tested on the same dataset and modality. Given the divergence in modality (multimodal vs. text-only), domain (open-world VQA vs. Quebec insurance), and pipeline scope (retrieval-only vs. retrieval+generation), no fair head-to-head ranking is possible without substantial re-running of one system in the other's setting.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers tackle fundamentally different problems: one answers questions that pair an image with the need for external world knowledge, while the other answers text-only questions about a specific body of Quebec automobile insurance documents. Their datasets, input modalities, target domains, and evaluation protocols have essentially no overlap, so placing their headline numbers side-by-side on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about relative quality that the underlying tasks do not support.

gold_rationale: Paper A (Think-on-Graph 2.0) tackles LLM reasoning hallucinations in knowledge-intensive QA by tightly coupling knowledge-graph traversal with retrieval-augmented generation, evaluated on multi-hop QA benchmarks with QA accuracy and reasoning faithfulness. Paper B (ReFIR) tackles hallucination/ungroundedness in large image restoration models by retrieving visually similar reference images, evaluated on image restoration benchmarks with image-quality scores (e.g., PSNR/SSIM/perceptual quality). All five coordinates diverge: the failure mode lives in different modalities (text reasoning vs. visual restoration), the evidence sources are structured KG triples vs. retrieved reference images, the pipeline insertion points are different (graph-guided reasoning steps vs. restoration backbone conditioning), and the evaluation targets share no common scale or benchmark. The only superficial commonality is the word 'retrieval-augmented.'
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to address the same task on shared benchmarks with comparable evaluation protocols. A direct ranking would require either (a) restricting comparison to a common retrieval-augmentation paradigm question on a shared task they both perform, or (b) treating them as instances of a general RAG-grounding strategy and comparing only at a conceptual/qualitative level rather than via a leaderboard. As stated, no shared task, benchmark, or scoring scale exists between text QA over KGs and image restoration.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works live in entirely different modalities and problem spaces: one is language reasoning over knowledge graphs for question answering, the other is visual restoration of images using reference look-ups. Their reported numbers come from disjoint benchmarks on incompatible scales, so placing them side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a comparison that simply does not exist and could lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about relative quality or progress that have no basis.

gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets provided), the two papers target fundamentally different research problems. Paper A addresses time-series grounding for multimodal embedding and retrieval, which implies a retrieval-style evaluation regime with similarity/ranking metrics over time-series-and-text pairs. Paper B addresses unified generative and discriminative training for multimodal LLMs, which implies vision-language benchmarks spanning generation and classification/retrieval-style discrimination. The failure types being addressed (lack of time-series-aware retrieval representations vs. siloed training objectives in MLLMs), the model components being changed (a time-series-text embedding pipeline vs. an MLLM training recipe), and the evaluation targets (time-series retrieval scores vs. multimodal LLM benchmark suites) are all distinct, so a head-to-head numerical ranking is not meaningful. Confidence is moderated because text snippets were unavailable and the inference rests only on titles.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on a shared benchmark with identical inputs (e.g., the same multimodal retrieval suite covering the same modality mix), identical evaluation protocol (same query/candidate construction, splits, and scoring), and overlapping target capabilities (both either doing time-series-grounded retrieval or both doing MLLM-style discriminative+generative tasks). At minimum, one paper would have to report results on a benchmark the other also reports, with matched modality coverage and matched metric definitions.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works appear to live in different research neighborhoods: one is about retrieving across time-series and text, the other is about training recipes for general multimodal large language models. Their headline numbers almost certainly come from different datasets, different scoring conventions, and different capability targets, so dropping them side by side in a single ranked table would give a reader a false sense that one system is 'better' than the other when in fact they are solving largely disjoint problems.

gold_rationale: No text snippets were supplied for either paper, so only the titles are available. From titles alone, Paper A ('Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling') appears to target the failure_type of LM generation quality/efficiency via a training-time distillation intervention over retrieved chunks, while Paper B ('Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation') appears to target context selection/ordering for RAG as an inference- or retriever-side intervention. The intervention_point is plausibly different (model parameters/distillation vs. context construction for an external generator), and we have no information about the evidence_assumption (training corpora, retrieval index, domain), metric_target (perplexity vs. downstream QA accuracy/faithfulness vs. retrieval metrics), or action_policy (deploy distilled LM vs. apply a context-tuning module). Without snippets we cannot verify that any single coordinate aligns, so a direct comparison cannot be responsibly adjudicated as valid, partial, or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: At minimum: (1) shared evaluation tasks and datasets, (2) overlapping metric_target (e.g., both reporting QA accuracy or both reporting LM perplexity on the same benchmark), (3) comparable base models and retrieval corpora so the evidence_assumption matches, (4) clarity that the intervention_point is contrasted on equal footing (e.g., both evaluated end-to-end with the same generator), and (5) matched action_policy framing (training-time modification vs. inference-time context manipulation should be normalized or controlled). Snippets or abstracts confirming these would be needed before placing the two on one leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: With only titles and no excerpts, a practitioner has no way to know whether the two systems were evaluated on the same tasks, datasets, base models, or scoring procedures. The titles hint at related but distinct research directions—one modifies how a language model is trained using retrieved text segments, the other modifies how surrounding context is prepared for a retrieval-augmented generator—so any side-by-side ranking would rest on guesses about the evaluation setups rather than verified common ground.

gold_rationale: Paper A provides only a title indicating a cooperative RAG approach using mutual information exchange and ranking by contrasting layers; no abstract or body text is available, so its datasets, retriever, base LLM, top-k, and reported scores are unknown. Paper B (WinnowRAG) is a model-agnostic multi-agent pipeline with query-aware clustering and a critic LLM that iteratively prunes noisy documents, with claims of effectiveness on 'various realistic datasets' but the snippet does not disclose which benchmarks, retrievers, or base LLMs. The two titles also suggest mechanisms at very different pipeline locations (intra-model layer contrasting versus multi-agent document filtering). Because Paper A's experimental coordinates are not observable, comparability cannot be verified along almost every dimension of the frame.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers must report on overlapping QA benchmarks (e.g., HotpotQA, NQ, TriviaQA, 2WikiMultihopQA), use the same retriever and corpus snapshot, the same generator LLM family and size, matched top-k retrieved documents, identical evaluation procedure (EM/F1 with same normalization), and disclosure of inference cost or document budget so that any quality gain is not confounded by additional compute. With Paper A's text missing, none of these can be confirmed.
independent_rubric_rationale: Because the first paper offers only a title and no body content, there is no way to confirm whether the datasets, retrievers, base models, top-k document budgets, or scoring procedures overlap with those used by the second paper. A practitioner placing the two headline numbers on a single leaderboard would have no basis for knowing whether the underlying experimental conditions actually line up.

gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets available), the two systems target orthogonal weaknesses of RAG pipelines. RankRAG addresses noisy or poorly ordered retrieved passages by unifying re-ranking and answer generation inside one LLM, so its primary headline numbers reflect end-task quality gains attributable to better context selection. xRAG addresses prompt length and serving cost by collapsing a passage into essentially a single embedding token via a projector aligned to a frozen LLM, so its headline numbers are an accuracy-vs-compression trade-off relative to a full-context baseline. The two thus differ on what is treated as the core defect of vanilla RAG (poor ordering vs. prohibitive context length), where in the pipeline they modify behavior (joint ranker-generator at decoding vs. encoder-side compression), what they primarily optimize against (downstream QA accuracy with longer ranked inputs vs. accuracy retention at extreme token budgets), and the runtime behavior of the resulting system (multi-passage reranking then generation vs. one-token-per-passage generation). They may share QA benchmarks such as NQ or TriviaQA, but a single leaderboard cell would suppress these very different cost/quality contracts.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A fair head-to-head would need (1) the same base LLM, retriever, and corpus; (2) matched evaluation suites with both accuracy and efficiency reported (input tokens consumed, latency, FLOPs, memory); (3) a Pareto view rather than a single scalar, because one method spends more compute for quality while the other spends quality for compute; (4) ablations that hold the number and form of retrieved passages constant; and (5) explicit statement of whether the comparison question is 'best accuracy at any cost' or 'best accuracy at a fixed token/latency budget'. Without these, ranking them on one number is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems are pursuing different goals: one is trying to squeeze more answer quality out of retrieved passages by reordering them, while the other is trying to make retrieval-augmented generation drastically cheaper by shrinking each passage to almost nothing. If a practitioner saw their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard, they would likely read it as 'A beats B' or vice versa on quality, and miss that the two are operating under very different cost budgets and were never aiming at the same target. Picking between them based on such a ranking would lead to wrong deployment decisions in most realistic settings.

gold_rationale: Both papers target the same broad failure_type — RAG performance degradation under noisy or irrelevant retrieved contexts — and both likely report QA benchmark accuracy as the metric_target. However, the intervention_point and action_policy differ substantially: SEER (Paper A) operates upstream by extracting and self-aligning evidence from retrieved passages before generation, whereas Neuro-RIT (Paper B) operates inside the generator LLM via neuron-level attribution and a two-stage instruction-tuning regime that selectively deactivates noise-responsive neurons. Their evidence_assumptions also diverge: SEER assumes a useful evidence span can be isolated from a passage, while Neuro-RIT assumes noise-vs-signal processing is sufficiently neuron-sparse to be disentangled. Comparison is therefore only partial — the goals overlap, but the mechanisms are at different layers of the pipeline and could in principle be complementary. The missing Paper A snippet, the implausible 2026 date and arXiv ID for Paper B, and the absence of shared benchmark/base-model details further weaken any direct head-to-head ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on the same QA benchmarks (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, PopQA) with the same base generator LLM, identical retriever and top-k retrieved contexts, matched noise injection protocols (e.g., same ratio of irrelevant or counterfactual passages), and the same answer-evaluation procedure (EM/F1). Ideally, an ablation showing whether SEER-style evidence extraction and Neuro-RIT-style neuron-guided tuning are substitutes or stack additively would be needed before placing them on one leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: Both papers aim to make retrieval-augmented generation more robust to noisy retrieved passages, but they operate at very different stages of the pipeline. SEER refines the retrieved evidence itself before it reaches the generator, while Neuro-RIT leaves retrieval alone and instead reshapes the generator model's internal neuron behavior through targeted tuning. If their headline numbers were placed side by side on one leaderboard, a practitioner could easily read them as direct alternatives and pick a 'winner,' when in reality the two techniques address different parts of the system and might even be combined. Without the SEER text snippet and without confirmation that the benchmarks, base LLMs, retrievers, and noise conditions line up, a clean ranking is not warranted, so the comparison is partly misleading rather than outright safe.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a survey/review paper cataloguing security threats, defenses, and benchmarks for RAG systems (data poisoning, adversarial attacks, membership inference, encryption, differential privacy, etc.). Paper B is the original Lewis et al. RAG method paper introducing a novel retrieval-augmented architecture and reporting empirical results on knowledge-intensive NLP benchmarks (open-domain QA, fact verification, etc.). These two works disagree on every coordinate: the failure_type addressed differs (security/privacy vulnerabilities vs. knowledge-intensive task accuracy/hallucination), the evidence_assumption differs (synthesized literature review vs. controlled empirical benchmark results), the intervention_point differs (defensive mechanisms across the RAG pipeline vs. a single proposed model architecture), the metric_target differs (security/robustness criteria vs. EM/F1 and generation quality on NLP benchmarks), and the action_policy differs (taxonomic guidance for future security work vs. a deployable model recipe). No common axis exists on which to rank them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to address the same problem (e.g., either both being RAG security surveys, or both proposing/evaluating a RAG method on the same NLP benchmark suite with shared metrics). At minimum, a shared evaluation dimension and overlapping evidence type would be needed before either ranking or head-to-head comparison could be meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing a security-focused survey of RAG threats and defenses next to the foundational paper that introduced RAG for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks on a single leaderboard would seriously confuse a practitioner. The two works answer fundamentally different questions, use incompatible kinds of evidence, and report numbers (when present) on entirely disjoint scales. Any side-by-side ranking would suggest a contest that does not exist.

gold_rationale: Both papers are non-empirical synthesis works addressing retrieval for LLMs, so they share topical territory (RAG, hallucination mitigation, retrieval quality). However, they diverge sharply on coordinates. Paper A is a broad comprehensive survey cataloging architectures (retriever-centric, generator-centric, hybrid, robustness-oriented) and enhancements across retrieval, filtering, decoding, and efficiency. Paper B is a perspective/position paper with a thesis-driven framing: denoising as the primary bottleneck, organized around a four-stage challenge framework (inaccessible→undiscoverable→misaligned→unverifiable). The evidence basis (broad synthesis vs. argued perspective), the recommended policy (taxonomic mapping vs. denoising-first prescription), and the success criteria (retrieval/QA performance trade-offs vs. signal-to-noise/verifiability) differ enough that placing the two side by side as equivalents would distort what each is trying to deliver.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) both works share genre (e.g., two comprehensive surveys of RAG with comparable taxonomy scope and inclusion criteria), or (b) they are framed as alternative syntheses of the same sub-question (e.g., denoising-focused review vs. broader review explicitly compared on coverage of the denoising literature, with date ranges, paper inclusion lists, and topical scope normalized). A direct ranking would also require an explicit dimension of comparison (coverage breadth, recency, taxonomic granularity, prescriptive guidance) rather than treating them as interchangeable references.
independent_rubric_rationale: A practitioner browsing both would find genuinely overlapping material on retrieval for language models, but the two pieces serve different purposes: one is a wide-angle reference catalog, the other is a thesis-driven essay advocating a particular lens on the field. Treating them as head-to-head entries on the same list would obscure that mismatch in genre and scope, though it would not produce an outright wrong takeaway, since both are credible reading on adjacent ground.

gold_rationale: Both papers are survey works addressing trustworthiness concerns in RAG systems and share a topical scope. However, their five-coordinate profiles diverge in important ways. Paper A organizes the literature around six perspectives (reliability, privacy, safety, fairness, explainability, accountability) and is purely descriptive/taxonomic, while Paper B organizes around six different (partially overlapping) dimensions (factuality, robustness, fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy) AND introduces an empirical evaluation benchmark (TRC Bench) with model comparisons. The evidence_assumption differs (literature synthesis only vs. literature plus empirical benchmarking), the metric_target differs (no quantitative metrics vs. benchmark scores across dimensions), and the action_policy differs (research roadmap only vs. roadmap plus benchmark-grounded model selection guidance). Failure_type is broadly aligned (trustworthiness risks of RAG) and intervention_point is similar (organizing the design space), so the comparison is not wholly invalid but is meaningfully partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid direct comparison would require (a) aligning the two taxonomies onto a shared set of trustworthiness dimensions, (b) treating Paper A strictly as a literature-organization contribution versus Paper B's literature plus benchmark contribution rather than collapsing them, and (c) restricting any head-to-head ranking to either coverage breadth/depth of the shared dimensions or to clearly separating the empirical benchmark contribution of Paper B from the taxonomy contributions of both.
independent_rubric_rationale: Both works are surveys on the same broad topic of trustworthy RAG, so a practitioner would reasonably expect them to be comparable. However, they use different category schemes with only partial overlap, and one of them adds an empirical leaderboard of model performance while the other stays purely descriptive. Placing their headline contributions side-by-side on a single ranking would give a practitioner a partly distorted view of what each work actually delivers.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a survey/taxonomy paper organizing the literature on RAG security threats and defenses along a six-stage knowledge-access pipeline (SLOT framework, CIA properties). Paper B (judging from title) is a concrete systems contribution proposing RAPID, a retrieval-augmented speculative decoding method for long-context inference efficiency. The two papers diverge on every coordinate: the failure_type differs (adversarial security breaches vs. latency/throughput of long-context generation); evidence_assumption differs (synthesis of prior attack/defense literature vs. empirical efficiency benchmarks); intervention_point differs (whole-pipeline taxonomic mapping vs. the decoding step with draft/verify); metric_target differs (confidentiality/integrity/availability outcomes vs. speed and generation-quality metrics); action_policy differs (an organizing framework with research-direction recommendations vs. a deployable algorithm). They share only the surface term 'retrieval-augmented' and cannot be placed on a common leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid pairing would require two artifacts addressing the same problem under comparable conditions, e.g., two RAG security taxonomies/surveys with overlapping scope and threat models, or two long-context inference methods evaluated on shared benchmarks (e.g., InfiniteBench, RULER) with reported latency, throughput, and quality numbers. At minimum, the two works should share the same outcome being measured and the same kind of contribution (survey-vs-survey or method-vs-method).
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper is a literature-organizing survey about security threats and protections in retrieval-augmented generation, while the other proposes a concrete decoding-time speed-up technique that uses retrieved content to draft tokens for long-context generation. They have different research goals, different deliverables (a taxonomy and research agenda versus an algorithm with speed/quality numbers), and no shared benchmark or scoring scheme. Putting their headline results side by side on a single leaderboard would give a practitioner a false impression that the two are addressing the same question or competing for the same slot.

gold_rationale: Paper A (SABER) is a defense-oriented method targeting natural PK/CK knowledge conflicts and unreliability; its failure_type is conflict-induced hallucination, its evidence_assumption is non-adversarial but possibly unreliable retrieved context, its intervention_point is inference-time belief estimation over already-retrieved evidence, its metric_target is end-to-end QA accuracy plus risk-coverage / abstention quality, and its action_policy is a 4-way choice among trust-PK / trust-CK / trust-either / abstain. Paper B (PoisonedRAG) is an offensive attack paper: failure_type is an adversarial security vulnerability of the corpus, evidence_assumption is an attacker injecting crafted malicious passages into the knowledge database, intervention_point is the retrieval corpus itself (data-poisoning), metric_target is attack success rate against target questions plus defense bypass, and action_policy is generating and injecting poisoned passages (with defenses as a secondary axis). All five coordinates diverge, and the two systems are not even on the same side of the problem (defender/abstainer vs. attacker).
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require both papers to be evaluated on the same task setup: e.g., run SABER as a defense against PoisonedRAG-style poisoned corpora and report a shared metric such as accuracy or attack-success-rate under the same retriever, LLM backbone, datasets, and poisoning budget. Alternatively, both would need to report results on a common knowledge-conflict-plus-poisoning benchmark with matched threat models. Without such a shared evaluation protocol, headline numbers (90% ASR vs. accuracy/abstention gains) refer to incompatible quantities.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper offers a defensive technique that lets the model choose among trusting its own memory, trusting the retrieved passage, or saying 'I don't know,' and reports correctness and selective-answering quality. The other paper is an offensive study that injects crafted poisoned passages into the corpus and reports how often the model is forced into the attacker's chosen wrong answer. Their headline numbers describe opposite goals on different evaluation pipelines, so a practitioner seeing them side by side on one leaderboard would draw incorrect conclusions about what either system delivers.

gold_rationale: The two papers address fundamentally distinct research problems within the RAG ecosystem. Paper A (Magic Mushroom) targets retrieval noise erosion: it builds a benchmark with four categories of misleading-but-surface-relevant noise and evaluates generators plus denoising strategies on QA accuracy under controlled noise distributions. Paper B (Axiomatic UE in RAG) targets uncertainty estimation: it proposes five axioms describing how UE scores should behave when retrieved documents are added, shows existing UE methods violate them, and proposes a calibration function judged by correlation between uncertainty and correctness. The failure modes (noise-induced wrong answers vs. miscalibrated confidence), assumed evidence regimes (heterogeneous noise categories vs. supportive/conflicting retrieved docs), points of change (benchmark design + denoiser choice vs. UE calibration), measured outcomes (answer correctness under noise vs. UE-correctness correlation and axiom satisfaction), and recommended next steps (build noise-robust generators/denoisers vs. build axiom-satisfying UE methods) all diverge. No coordinate aligns sufficiently to support direct comparison or ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to share at least the same outcome being scored and the same kind of system change being proposed, e.g., both reporting QA accuracy under matched retrieval-noise conditions on overlapping datasets and LLMs, or both reporting UE-correctness correlation on the same RAG configurations. Minimally, one would need a common benchmark, identical evaluation metric, and comparable system components (generator, retriever, and either denoiser or UE module) so that a leaderboard entry reflects the same underlying quantity.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works speak to disjoint practitioner questions. One asks how well a generator preserves answer quality when retrieved passages are deceptive; the other asks how well a confidence score tracks correctness once retrieval is added to the prompt. Putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would conflate answer quality with confidence calibration, and a reader could easily infer a ranking that has no operational meaning, leading to wrong tooling choices.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic/benchmark contribution: it characterizes three problematic retrieval scenarios (unanswerable, adversarial, conflicting), proposes a new attack generator (GenADV) and a new robustness metric (RAD), and reports how existing RALMs degrade. Paper B is a model-training contribution: it proposes RoseRAG, a margin-aware preference optimization pipeline (multi-turn prompting, rejection sampling, contrastive preference selection) to make small-scale LLMs more robust on three open-domain QA benchmarks, reporting EM/F1 against SOTA baselines. They differ on what they perturb (diverse scenario taxonomy with custom adversarial generation vs. generic noisy/retrieved-document setting), where they act (no model change, evaluation only vs. preference-based fine-tuning of SLMs), what they measure (RAD plus scenario-detection behavior vs. EM/F1 on HotpotQA-style tasks), and what they ultimately deliver (diagnostic framework vs. trained robust model). Only the broad framing of 'imperfect retrieval' is shared.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) running RoseRAG and an equivalent baseline through Paper A's scenario suite using the same backbone models and reporting RAD plus unanswerable/conflict detection behavior, or (b) running Paper A's evaluated RALMs through Paper B's three QA benchmarks under matched retrievers, k, and EM/F1 protocol. Without aligning model scale, retrieval pipeline, perturbation distribution, and the reported metric, the two headline numbers refer to different quantities.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper delivers a diagnostic study with a custom robustness score on hand-crafted problematic document sets, while the other delivers a trained small-model system reporting standard exact-match and F1 on open-domain QA. Putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest the two systems were solving the same task under the same conditions, when in fact the benchmarks, the backbones, the document perturbations, and the scoring quantities are all different, so a practitioner choosing between them based on such a table would draw conclusions that the underlying experiments do not support.

gold_rationale: Paper A targets complex multi-step task planning, using a knowledge graph as structured evidence and inserting symbolic verification at the planning/decomposition stage to validate plan steps. Paper B targets noisy or misleading passages retrieved during open-domain QA-style RAG, using unstructured retrieved text as evidence and inserting a learned rewriter (DPO-trained on a supportiveness signal) as a preprocessing module before generation. The two systems therefore differ on every coordinate: the failure they address (planning errors vs. retrieval noise), the evidence form they assume (KG triples/subgraphs vs. text passages), the pipeline locus of the fix (plan synthesis/verification vs. context rewriting), the reported metric family (plan/task success on complex-task benchmarks vs. accuracy on knowledge-intensive QA across multiple LLMs), and the policy itself (hierarchical decomposition + symbolic check vs. supportiveness-aligned text summarization). With no Paper A text snippet available, some details are inferred from the title, but the gap is wide enough on multiple coordinates that direct comparison is not warranted.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to (a) tackle the same class of failure on a shared benchmark, (b) operate over the same evidence representation (either both KG-grounded or both text-passage RAG), (c) intervene at a comparable pipeline stage, (d) report a common, head-to-head metric (e.g., the same QA set or the same complex-task planning suite), and (e) ideally hold the backbone LLM and retriever constant. Absent shared benchmarks and a common pipeline locus, any side-by-side ranking is meaningless.
