independent_rubric_rationale: These two systems tackle distinct problems—one decomposes and verifies multi-step plans grounded in a structured knowledge graph, while the other rewrites noisy retrieved passages so a language model can answer questions better. They consume different kinds of source information (graph-structured facts versus unstructured text), operate at different stages of the pipeline, and report numbers on different benchmark families. Placing their headline scores side by side on one leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head contest that does not exist, and a practitioner could easily pick the wrong tool for their actual use case.

gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive security study targeting indirect prompt injection in RAG/agentic pipelines; its failure_type is adversarial corpus poisoning, its evidence_assumption is an attacker with embedding-API access and write access to the external corpus, its intervention_point is the document/corpus side (trigger+attack fragment construction), its metric_target is retrieval rate and end-to-end attack success (e.g., SSH-key exfiltration ~80%), and its action_policy is a black-box attack algorithm. Paper B is a defensive RL training method for grounded answering and abstention; its failure_type is hallucination and ungrounded answering under insufficient evidence, its evidence_assumption is a benign retriever returning mixed-sufficiency contexts, its intervention_point is generator fine-tuning via multi-stage gated rewards, its metric_target is answer accuracy plus calibrated abstention, and its action_policy is producing grounded answers or explicit 'I don't know'. The two works share only the RAG substrate; every coordinate diverges.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would require both papers to address the same failure mode (e.g., either both attacking retrieval or both improving grounding under adversarial/noisy contexts), operate on a shared threat or evidence model, intervene at compatible pipeline stages, and report at least one common headline number (e.g., attack-success-rate of poisoned content versus abstention-on-poisoned-content for a defense, on a shared benchmark and embedding model). Without an overlapping setup such as evaluating GRACE-style abstention against IPI-poisoned corpora, no meaningful ranking is possible.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placed side by side on one leaderboard, a practitioner would be seriously misled: one paper reports how often a hidden adversarial document gets pulled in and hijacks the model, while the other reports how often a model gives a correct grounded answer or politely declines on benign question-answering benchmarks. The headline numbers measure different worlds (offense versus reliability), use different datasets and threat conditions, and have no shared baseline, so any direct ordering would suggest a comparison that does not exist.

gold_rationale: Paper A addresses naturally occurring knowledge conflicts in RAG (temporal shifts, debatable/controversial queries, differing perspectives) where all sources may be legitimate, and proposes a taxonomy plus prompting strategies whose success is judged by response appropriateness per conflict type. Paper B addresses adversarial knowledge corruption (data poisoning) where attackers inject malicious passages into the retrieval pool, and proposes a lightweight post-retrieval filter judged by Attack Success Rate reduction. The failure modes (benign disagreement vs. malicious injection), the evidence model (all legitimate vs. partially adversarial), the pipeline stage of the fix (generation-time prompting vs. post-retrieval filtering), the success metric, and the desired model behavior (nuanced multi-perspective answers vs. discard-and-answer-from-clean-set) all differ. They cannot be placed on a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on the same problem scope (either natural conflict resolution or adversarial corruption defense), using a shared benchmark with comparable ground-truth labels, the same retrieval pipeline and base LLMs, and a common scoring criterion (e.g., both judged on ASR under poisoning, or both judged on conflict-type-appropriate response quality on a benchmark like CONFLICTS). At minimum, Paper B would need to be run on natural-conflict data or Paper A's prompting approach would need to be evaluated under poisoning attacks with ASR reporting.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works look superficially similar because both involve 'conflicts' among retrieved passages in RAG, but they target fundamentally different scenarios. One handles genuine disagreement among legitimate sources (outdated info, debatable topics) and aims to produce well-calibrated, possibly multi-perspective answers. The other defends against attackers who deliberately seed the corpus with poisoned passages and aims to discard them before answering. A practitioner glancing at a shared leaderboard could easily pick the wrong tool: deploying the poisoning-defense filter on a debatable-opinion query would suppress legitimate minority viewpoints, and using the conflict-acknowledgment prompting on a poisoned corpus would amplify attacker content. The headline numbers (response-quality scores vs. attack-success-rate) are not on the same scale or about the same phenomenon.

gold_rationale: Paper A (RoseRAG) targets noise-robust answer generation in small-scale LLMs via margin-aware preference optimization, reporting QA quality scores such as Exact Match and F1 on open-domain QA benchmarks. Paper B (FRANQ) targets hallucination detection in RAG outputs via uncertainty quantification, with an explicit distinction between faithfulness and factuality, evaluated as a detection task on a new long-form QA dataset. The two works differ on essentially every coordinate: what counts as the problem (noise-induced wrong answers vs. unfaithful/non-factual claims), what is done about it (training-time preference optimization vs. post-hoc per-statement scoring), the locus of the change (the generator itself vs. an external verifier), and what is reported (generation quality scores vs. error-detection performance). They therefore cannot be ranked on a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A common task definition (either both improving generation quality on the same QA benchmarks with the same retriever and base model, or both producing per-claim hallucination scores evaluated with the same detection metric on the same annotated dataset), matched base LLMs, identical retrieval corpus and top-K, and a shared scoring protocol. Without aligning at least the task output type (free-form answer vs. uncertainty score) and the evaluation metric family (QA quality vs. detection AUC/PR), no direct ranking is meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers solve fundamentally different problems with different outputs and different evaluation numbers. One reports how well a small model answers open-domain questions after fine-tuning, while the other reports how well a scoring procedure flags unsupported or incorrect claims in already-generated text. Putting their headline numbers side by side on one table would suggest a head-to-head winner where none exists, and a practitioner choosing between them on that basis would draw incorrect conclusions about which is better for their use case.

gold_rationale: Paper A targets the misalignment of classical IR ranking metrics (nDCG, MAP, MRR) with LLM-as-consumer behavior in RAG, proposing UDCG, a utility/distraction-aware metric evaluated by correlation with end-to-end RAG answer accuracy across five datasets and six LLMs. Paper B (title only: 'Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling') concerns a language modeling technique involving chunk-level distillation; this is a generative modeling contribution rather than a retrieval evaluation metric. The two works differ on essentially every coordinate: the problem being solved (retrieval-evaluation misalignment vs. LM modeling/efficiency), where the change is made (offline IR scoring vs. LM training/inference), the quantity being optimized (rank-quality/accuracy correlation vs. likely perplexity or generation quality), and the deliverable (a scoring metric vs. a modeling method). Without Paper B's snippet I cannot fully verify its evaluation setup, but the title alone makes the comparison category-mismatched.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to address the same task family (e.g., both proposing RAG components evaluated on the same QA benchmarks with the same LLM readers), use comparable evaluation targets (e.g., end-to-end answer accuracy or the same retrieval-quality correlation), and produce artifacts of the same type (either two metrics evaluated by correlation with downstream accuracy, or two retrieval/LM components evaluated on accuracy). A direct comparison would also require shared datasets, shared LLM backbones, and consistent reporting (e.g., the same accuracy/EM/F1 figures), none of which appear shared here.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works live in different research categories: one delivers a new scoring tool for judging retrieved passages in RAG and is validated by how well its scores track downstream answer correctness, while the other contributes a chunk-based language modeling approach whose headline numbers would naturally be generation-quality scores. Putting their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head contest that does not actually exist, and a practitioner trying to choose between them for a real system would be drawing a conclusion the underlying evidence cannot support.

gold_rationale: Based on titles and venues alone (no snippets available), Paper A (LI-RAGE) targets open-domain Table Question Answering using late-interaction retrieval over structured tables, while Paper B (DSLR) targets text-passage RAG via post-retrieval sentence-level reranking and reconstruction. The failure_type differs (table retrieval matching vs. noisy/irrelevant sentences in retrieved passages); the evidence_assumption differs (structured tabular cells vs. unstructured prose passages); the intervention_point differs (retriever architecture with explicit signals vs. post-retrieval document refinement); and the metric_target almost certainly differs (table-QA benchmarks like NQ-tables/OTT-QA vs. open-domain text QA benchmarks). The action_policy is also different in spirit (retrieve-better vs. clean-after-retrieval). They are not on a shared evaluation surface.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both systems to be evaluated on the same benchmark with the same evidence modality (e.g., either both on open-domain text QA or both on table QA), the same retriever/corpus setup, and the same end-task metrics, ideally with one paper's technique reimplemented or ablated within the other's pipeline so the contribution being compared is isolated. Without shared datasets, modality, and evaluation protocol, head-to-head ranking is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems address fundamentally different inputs and pipeline stages: one works with structured tables in an open-domain table QA pipeline, the other cleans up unstructured text passages before generation. Putting their headline numbers next to each other on a single leaderboard would conflate distinct task settings, corpora, and evaluation suites, leading a practitioner to draw unsupported conclusions about which approach is 'better' for retrieval-augmented generation.

gold_rationale: The two papers diverge on essentially every coordinate. Paper A (TrustRAG) addresses an adversarial failure mode — corpus poisoning attacks where malicious documents are deliberately injected into the retrieval corpus (PoisonedRAG-style threat model) — and intervenes by filtering retrieved documents through cluster analysis plus LLM self-assessment, with primary metrics around attack resistance and robustness under adversarial evidence. Paper B (SUGAR) addresses a benign efficiency/noise failure mode — that always-on retrieval is wasteful and that noisy but non-adversarial retrieved content can distract the model — and intervenes upstream of retrieval by using semantic-entropy-based confidence to decide whether to retrieve at all and whether to do single- vs multi-step retrieval, with metrics around QA accuracy and inference efficiency on standard (non-poisoned) QA benchmarks. The evidence regimes (adversarial vs clean), the policy levers (post-retrieval filtering vs pre-retrieval gating), and the leaderboards on which each would naturally be scored are non-overlapping.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation in which both systems are run on the same QA benchmarks under matched conditions covering both (a) a clean / standard retrieval setting and (b) a poisoned-corpus setting, using the same retriever and base LLM, and reporting both attack-robustness scores (e.g., attack success rate, accuracy under PoisonedRAG-style injection) and efficiency/quality scores (e.g., retrieval-call rate, end-task accuracy, latency). Without that joint protocol — or at minimum a clear declaration that the two systems target distinct sub-problems and are not in competition — they cannot be ranked head-to-head.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems solve different problems within RAG: one defends against deliberately poisoned documents in the corpus, the other decides when retrieval is even worth doing and how deep it should go, evaluated on ordinary question-answering. Their reported numbers come from different benchmarks, different threat conditions, and different success criteria, so a practitioner who saw the headline scores placed on one shared ranking would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is stronger or more appropriate for their deployment.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a controlled behavioral study of how LLMs handle benign/organic knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and external evidence, measuring receptiveness and confirmation bias using constructed counter-memory. Paper B is an adversarial security study proposing GRAGPOISON, a poisoning attack against GraphRAG systems that exploits shared relations in knowledge graphs, measured by attack success rate (up to 98%) and poisoning-text efficiency. The two works diverge on every coordinate: the failure being characterized (organic conflict vs. malicious poisoning), the nature of the external evidence (coherent counter-memory from elicited parametric beliefs vs. adversary-crafted text), the locus of study (LLM consumption behavior vs. graph indexing/retrieval pipeline of GraphRAG specifically), the outcome being measured (receptiveness/bias percentages vs. attack success and stealth), and the stance of the work (descriptive analysis vs. offensive method with defense discussion). They also evaluate on different system architectures (vanilla tool-augmented LLMs vs. GraphRAG variants).
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to study the same threat or phenomenon (e.g., both adversarial poisoning, or both benign conflict), on overlapping system architectures (e.g., both on GraphRAG or both on standard RAG), with shared outcome measures (e.g., attack success rate on the same task, or a common receptiveness/robustness metric on the same benchmark), and a shared role (both as attack methods, both as analyses, or both as defenses). At minimum, one would need a common evaluation setup with the same datasets, models, and a metric that captures comparable quantities.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing these two results side by side on a single leaderboard would mislead a practitioner because the two studies are addressing fundamentally different questions on different systems with different threat models. Paper A's percentages describe how a model naturally weighs conflicting context elicited from its own beliefs, while Paper B's percentages describe how often an adversary can corrupt a graph-structured retrieval pipeline. Numbers like 'receptiveness' and 'attack success rate' look superficially like comparable rates but encode incompatible quantities, so a reader could wrongly infer that one work outperforms or supersedes the other when they do not address the same problem at all.

gold_rationale: Paper A proposes a decoding-time technique (Adaptive Contrastive Decoding) targeting answer correctness in open-domain QA when retrieved context is noisy but the query is in principle answerable. Paper B is an evaluation library plus benchmark (knowornot / PolicyBench) targeting whether LLMs appropriately abstain on out-of-knowledge-base queries. The two works diverge on what counts as a failure (wrong answer under distractor context vs. answering at all when no supporting evidence exists), on the evidence regime (in-scope retrieval with noise vs. deliberately out-of-scope queries), on the locus of contribution (model decoding modification vs. evaluation tooling and benchmark), on what is scored (QA correctness vs. abstention/OOKB robustness), and on the desired model behavior (answer better vs. refuse to answer). Only the 'evidence_assumption' coordinate has any overlap, and even there the regimes differ.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require (1) a shared task definition that includes both answerable-with-noise and unanswerable/OOKB queries, (2) a shared scoring scheme that jointly rewards correct answers and correct abstentions (e.g., a selective-QA or risk-coverage metric), (3) running Paper A's ACD inside Paper B's evaluation pipeline on PolicyBench (or running an abstention-capable variant of ACD on the same dataset), and (4) matched models, retrievers, prompts, and decoding budgets. Without these, the methods sit in disjoint evaluation frames.
independent_rubric_rationale: Dropping the headline numbers of these two works into a single leaderboard would seriously mislead a practitioner. One paper reports gains on answering open-domain questions when retrieved passages contain distractors; the other reports how well systems decline to respond when the knowledge base does not actually cover the query. A reader scanning a unified table would not see that the two systems are being judged on incompatible goals (getting the right answer vs. correctly refusing), on different datasets, and with different success criteria, and could easily conclude one is 'better' than the other when they are addressing essentially different problems.

gold_rationale: Paper A (SeedRG) is a benchmark-generation pipeline that addresses knowledge leakage in RAG evaluation; its failure type is unreliable evaluation due to parametric-memory contamination, its intervention point is the benchmark/data layer, its metric targets are leakage reduction and discriminative power across RAG systems, and its deliverable is an evaluation artifact. Paper B (Superposition Prompting) is a prompting/inference-time technique aimed at improving accuracy and latency of RAG; its failure type is suboptimal RAG quality/speed, its intervention point is the prompt-construction/inference layer, its metric targets are answer quality and runtime, and its deliverable is a method to deploy. The two contributions operate at different layers of the RAG stack and report fundamentally different quantities, so a direct head-to-head ranking is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both works to deliver the same kind of contribution evaluated on the same axis — e.g., both being RAG methods evaluated on a shared, leakage-controlled benchmark with matched retrievers, generators, and reported under the same accuracy/latency definitions. Alternatively, Superposition Prompting could be re-evaluated on SeedRG-generated tasks alongside other RAG methods, but this still would not put the benchmark itself and the method on the same leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: Paper A delivers a leakage-controlled evaluation dataset whose headline numbers describe how much contamination is removed and how clearly RAG systems can then be distinguished, while Paper B delivers a prompting/inference technique whose headline numbers describe answer quality and speed improvements over baseline RAG pipelines. These are different kinds of deliverables measured on different quantities, so a practitioner who saw their top-line scores listed together on one leaderboard would likely draw incorrect conclusions about which is 'better,' since neither is a substitute for the other.

gold_rationale: judgment based on titles only since no snippets were provided. The two papers share the 'RAG' label but operate in entirely disjoint problem spaces. Paper A targets neural symbolic regression — recovering closed-form mathematical expressions fitting numerical data — using retrieval over an expression library. Paper B targets long-term memory for LLMs in knowledge-intensive QA, using a neurobiologically inspired indexing structure over text corpora. All five coordinates diverge: the failure modes addressed (poor symbolic search vs. weak multi-hop knowledge integration), the underlying evidence (regression datasets vs. text/QA corpora), the intervention point (expression generation loop vs. memory indexing and retrieval), the metric targets (regression error / expression quality vs. QA accuracy / multi-hop reasoning), and the recommended action policy each support are unrelated.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require both systems to be evaluated on the same task family (e.g., both on symbolic regression benchmarks like SRBench, or both on multi-hop QA like MuSiQue / 2WikiMultiHopQA), under matched retrieval corpora, comparable backbone models, and a shared primary metric. Absent any common benchmark, dataset, or task definition, no leaderboard placement can be meaningfully constructed.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle fundamentally different problems — discovering mathematical formulas that fit numerical data versus equipping language models with durable knowledge stores for question answering. Because they share only the surface-level 'retrieval-augmented' branding, putting their headline numbers side by side on one ranking would strongly suggest a comparability that does not exist, and a practitioner skimming such a table could easily draw unfounded conclusions about which approach is 'better'.

gold_rationale: Paper A (GMTP) targets adversarial corpus poisoning in RAG, defending retrieval via gradient-based masked token probability filtering, with success measured by poisoned-document detection/filtering rates and preserved retrieval quality under attack. Paper B addresses personalization of agents via editable memory graphs over user data, with success measured by personalization or response quality on benign user contexts. The two operate on disjoint problem framings (security vs. personalization), assume different threat/data conditions (adversarial injections vs. trusted user memory), modify different pipeline stages (pre-retrieval filtering vs. memory-graph construction/editing), optimize incomparable metrics, and produce different system behaviors. Note: Paper B snippet is unavailable, but the title is unambiguous enough about scope to support an invalid verdict rather than underspecified.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task and evaluation setting where both methods are run on the same RAG benchmark under the same conditions, with a common metric of interest. For example, evaluating GMTP and the memory-graph personalization system on identical poisoned-corpus benchmarks with end-task accuracy under attack, or on identical personalization benchmarks with and without injected adversarial documents. Without such overlap in problem definition, threat model, evaluation corpus, and headline metric, any side-by-side ranking would be meaningless.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems address fundamentally different goals on different data regimes: one protects retrieval against adversarial injections, the other tailors agent responses to a user's editable memory. Their headline numbers come from incompatible benchmarks and score different things, so placing them next to each other on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about relative quality that the underlying experiments do not support.

gold_rationale: Paper A (TCR) targets benign knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and noisy retrieved context, treating the failure_type as hallucination/over-trust on non-adversarial snippets; its evidence_assumption is that retrieved passages may be inconsistent but not maliciously crafted. Its intervention_point is signal injection through dual contrastive encoders plus a soft-prompt, and its metric_target is conflict-detection F1, knowledge-gap recovery (+21.4 pp), and misleading-context overrides (-29.3 pp) across seven benchmarks; the action_policy is a plug-and-play 0.3%-parameter add-on. Paper B (CORDON-MAS) targets adversarial Confundo-style poisoning; evidence_assumption is that documents are optimized to survive the pipeline. Its intervention_point is architectural compartmentalization across Extractor/Auditor/Gate/Synthesizer agents with asymmetric memory privileges, its metric_target is attack success rate reduction (92.4% relative) on five BEIR datasets, and its action_policy is a full multi-agent system redesign. All five coordinates diverge, and the benchmarks and headline numbers measure incompatible quantities.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared threat model (either both benign conflict or both adversarial poisoning), a common benchmark suite and retriever/generator stack, a shared primary metric (e.g., both reporting attack success rate under the same poisoning protocol, or both reporting conflict-resolution accuracy on the same conflict corpora), matched compute/parameter budgets, and ideally a cross-evaluation where each method is tested on the other's threat (e.g., TCR under Confundo attacks; CORDON-MAS on benign noisy-context QA).
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems are solving different problems on different datasets with different headline numbers: one reports gains on conflict-detection F1 and override reduction across seven QA-style benchmarks against non-adversarial noisy context, while the other reports a 92.4% relative drop in adversarial poisoning success across five BEIR datasets. Putting these side by side on a single leaderboard would let a reader infer that one approach 'outperforms' the other when in fact they have not been evaluated under the same conditions or against the same threat, so a practitioner choosing between them based on the reported numbers would draw an unsupported conclusion.

gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets available), Paper A targets robustness of the generator to defective retrieval results via fine-tuning, while Paper B targets improving retrieval quality in the biomedical domain via a self-rewarding tree search procedure at inference. These differ on the failure_type addressed (corrupted/noisy retrieved evidence vs. suboptimal retrieval pathing), the intervention_point (offline fine-tuning of the generator vs. inference-time search over retrieval candidates), the evidence_assumption (general-domain corpus vs. biomedical corpus), and the metric_target (general RAG robustness benchmarks vs. biomedical QA benchmarks). The action_policy also diverges (train-once weights update vs. per-query search policy). Note: judgment based solely on titles; no abstracts or results were available.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful head-to-head would require both systems to be evaluated on the same corpus and task (e.g., both on biomedical QA or both on a shared robustness-to-noisy-retrieval benchmark), with the same retriever held constant, the same evaluation metrics, and a matched threat model (either both stressed with injected retrieval defects, or both evaluated under clean retrieval). Ideally one would also report compute costs since inference-time search and fine-tuning have very different deployment profiles.
independent_rubric_rationale: If a practitioner saw these two systems side by side on one leaderboard, they would likely draw the wrong conclusion. The two works tackle different problems in retrieval-augmented generation: one hardens the generator to cope with low-quality retrieved passages in a general setting, while the other reshapes the search procedure used to find biomedical passages. They almost certainly run on different datasets, different base models, and different evaluation suites, so a single ranked number would conflate domain, technique, and deployment cost rather than tell the reader which system is 'better'.

gold_rationale: Even with Paper A's snippet missing, the titles and Paper B's abstract make the divergence clear. Paper A targets a specific error-detection problem (hallucination and coverage errors) within a narrow domain (controversial topics) in RAG. Paper B is a general-purpose benchmark for retrieval-noise robustness, defining four noise categories and evaluating generators and denoising strategies under configurable noise mixtures. The failure_type differs (hallucination/coverage vs. noise-induced degradation); the evidence_assumption differs (retrieved passages on contested topics vs. crafted heterogeneous noise distributions); the intervention_point differs (a detection step vs. an end-to-end evaluation harness); the metric_target differs (detection precision/recall-style scores vs. QA accuracy or robustness under noise); and the action_policy differs (flag suspicious outputs vs. rank generators/denoisers on a benchmark). These do not map onto a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to address the same task framing on overlapping data (e.g., both detecting hallucination in RAG outputs, or both benchmarking generation quality under noisy retrieval), report the same evaluation scores on the same instances or splits, and apply consistent definitions of correctness and noise. At minimum, a shared evaluation set, identical scoring protocol, and matched task definition would be required before juxtaposing headline numbers.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works address quite different questions about RAG. One is about spotting answer errors on contested or debated subjects, while the other is a configurable testbed for studying how various kinds of plausible-looking but unhelpful retrieved passages erode answer quality. Placing their headline numbers side by side on a single ranking would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions the underlying studies do not support, because the two report different kinds of scores on different problem setups.

gold_rationale: The two works share only the broad RAG umbrella and diverge on every coordinate. Paper A targets text-to-SQL generation over electronic health records for epidemiological questions, where the failure_type is incorrect SQL/query formulation and the evidence_assumption is structured EHR schemas with retrieved example queries; its intervention_point is prompt-level retrieval augmentation, its metric_target is SQL execution correctness in a clinical domain, and its action_policy is retrieve-then-generate-SQL. Paper B targets general open-domain QA with RALMs, where the failure_type is generator distraction by noisy/irrelevant passages, the evidence_assumption is unstructured retrieved documents that may be noisy, the intervention_point is neuron-level parameter updates via attribution-based mining and two-stage instruction tuning, the metric_target is QA accuracy on general benchmarks, and the action_policy is a tuned generator with selectively deactivated neurons. No coordinate aligns.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both systems to be evaluated on the same task (e.g., either both on text-to-SQL over EHRs or both on open-domain QA), with a shared dataset, shared retrieval setup, and a shared evaluation protocol/metric. Additionally, the noise/robustness conditions and the training regime (instruction tuning vs in-context retrieval prompting) would need to be controlled or at least reported on comparable axes.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing these two results side by side on a single leaderboard would seriously mislead a practitioner because the systems solve different problems on different data with different scoring conventions. One produces executable SQL against clinical databases for epidemiology questions; the other produces natural-language answers on general knowledge benchmarks while being hardened against noisy passages. Any apparent ordering between their headline numbers would reflect task and dataset differences, not the relative quality of the systems.

gold_rationale: Paper A is an adversarial security study that proposes a coordinated prompt-and-corpus poisoning attack on RAG pipelines, formulated as bilevel optimization, and evaluated by attack success rate and stealth under a threat model assuming an attacker can inject poisoned passages and a backdoor trigger. Paper B is a benign capability/efficiency study comparing RAG to long-context LLMs and proposing a hybrid routing approach, evaluated on QA-style accuracy/cost trade-offs under standard non-adversarial conditions. The two works diagnose different problems (security vulnerability vs. architectural performance trade-off), operate under incompatible evidence regimes (adversarial vs. benign), modify different parts of the pipeline (attacker-injected poisoned passages/triggers vs. retriever/long-context routing), optimize incomparable scoring quantities (ASR/stealth vs. answer quality/efficiency), and prescribe different downstream choices (defense awareness vs. system design selection). No coordinate aligns.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful side-by-side comparison would require both papers to study the same task under the same conditions—e.g., both reporting QA accuracy on shared benchmarks under matched retrieval setups, or both reporting robustness under the same adversarial threat model with the same poisoning budget. Alternatively, one would need a defense-vs-attack framing where Paper B's hybrid approach was evaluated against Paper A's PR-Attack on identical datasets, retrievers, and LLM backbones with shared evaluation protocols.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works answer fundamentally different questions about retrieval-augmented systems—one quantifies how easily a malicious party can corrupt outputs, the other quantifies how well different system designs answer questions efficiently under normal use. Their headline numbers are measured on incomparable scales and under opposite operating conditions, so dropping them into a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw a comparison that the underlying studies do not support.

gold_rationale: Paper A targets a benign failure_type (contextual unfaithfulness where the LLM ignores or conflicts with retrieved context) under the evidence_assumption that retrieval may contain natural noise or knowledge-conflict; its intervention_point is the LLM's internal latent space (pruning, latent probing, attention modulation); its metric_target is QA accuracy and faithfulness; its action_policy is to defend/improve generation. Paper B targets an adversarial failure_type (opinion manipulation of RAG outputs) under the evidence_assumption that an attacker can inject a few poisoned documents into the corpus and only black-box access to the retriever exists; its intervention_point is the document corpus via surrogate-retriever-guided triggers; its metric_target is attack success rate, opinion-polarity shift, and downstream user-cognition shift; its action_policy is offensive red-teaming. All five coordinates diverge, so no shared leaderboard exists.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would require both papers to address the same problem framing: e.g., (1) the same threat or quality model (either both defending against adversarial corpus poisoning for opinion manipulation, or both improving faithfulness to clean-but-noisy context), (2) shared datasets and query types (controversial opinion queries vs. factoid QA), (3) a common evaluation suite reporting comparable numbers (e.g., faithfulness/accuracy under the same noise regime, or attack-success/defense-success rates against the same poisoning pipeline), and (4) compatible operating assumptions about access to model internals (ProbeRAG needs white-box hidden states; FlippedRAG assumes a fully black-box target). Without realigning on at least the problem definition and metrics, ranking them is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works study essentially opposite questions: one builds a defender-side technique that uses model internals to keep answers consistent with retrieved passages, while the other is a red-team study showing how a few poisoned documents can steer opinions in answers produced by a black-box system. Their headline numbers (a faithfulness/accuracy gain on QA benchmarks versus a ~50% opinion-polarity shift and ~20% user-cognition shift from a successful attack) live in different units, on different datasets, with different threat models, and aim at different outcomes. A practitioner reading them on a single leaderboard would almost certainly draw wrong conclusions about which system is 'better' for any concrete deployment.

gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets provided), the two papers address fundamentally different problems within the broad RAG umbrella. Paper A is a benchmark contribution targeting cross-lingual and culturally-sensitive robustness in multilingual RAG, evaluating how existing systems behave across languages and cultural contexts. Paper B is a model-side method paper proposing a robust fine-tuning recipe to harden RAG against retrieval defects (e.g., noisy or irrelevant passages), almost certainly in a monolingual setting. The failure modes (cultural/cross-lingual misalignment vs. defective retrieval), the evidence corpora assumed (multilingual culturally grounded sources vs. defect-laden monolingual retrievals), the locus of change (dataset/benchmark vs. training-time fine-tuning), the headline numbers (cross-lingual consistency/cultural accuracy vs. defect-robustness scores), and the deliverable (evaluation resource vs. trained model recipe) all diverge. Placing them on the same leaderboard would conflate distinct research artifacts.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) both papers evaluated on a shared task with the same robustness perturbations and the same languages/corpora, or (b) Paper B's fine-tuning recipe re-run and scored on Paper A's multilingual culturally-sensitive benchmark (or vice versa, Paper A's measured systems stressed under Paper B's retrieval-defect protocol). Shared base models, retrieval corpora, defect taxonomy, and reported scores under matched conditions would be needed before any side-by-side ranking is meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper delivers a multilingual, culturally-grounded evaluation resource and reports how systems behave across languages, while the other delivers a training recipe meant to harden a model against noisy or wrong retrieved passages in what is almost certainly a monolingual setup. Putting their headline numbers next to each other on a single leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head comparison that does not exist: the tasks, data, languages, and the kind of stress being probed are different, so a practitioner reading such a leaderboard could easily draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is 'better' for their use case.

gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets provided), the two works target fundamentally different problem settings. Paper A concerns a training-time unification of generative and discriminative objectives for multi-modal LLMs, presumably evaluated on vision-language benchmarks. Paper B concerns inference-time acceleration of retrieval-augmented generation via sparse context selection, presumably evaluated on RAG QA benchmarks with latency/throughput as primary outcomes. The five coordinates diverge: the problem being addressed (multi-modal capability gap vs. RAG inference cost), the empirical evidence base (MLLM benchmarks vs. RAG corpora), where the change is made (training procedure vs. inference-time context pruning), what is being optimized (task accuracy across modalities vs. speed/efficiency at iso-quality), and the deployment scenario the recommendation supports.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful side-by-side comparison would require both works to address the same problem class (e.g., both proposing inference-time efficiency techniques for the same model family on overlapping benchmarks, or both proposing training schemes evaluated on shared multi-modal tasks), use compatible evaluation suites with shared baselines, and report outcomes on the same primary axes (e.g., quality at matched compute, or speedup at matched accuracy). None of these conditions appear satisfied here.
independent_rubric_rationale: If a practitioner saw the headline numbers from these two papers placed on a single leaderboard, they would likely draw incorrect conclusions, because the works solve unrelated problems on different data with different success criteria. One concerns how a multi-modal model is taught to handle both producing and discriminating content; the other concerns how to make a retrieval-based pipeline faster at serving time. Ranking them together has no operational meaning for a downstream user choosing between them.

gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive security study proposing a black-box adversarial framework (CPA-RAG) that poisons the retrieval corpus to induce target answers, evaluated by Attack Success Rate. Paper B is a defensive alignment study (DTA) that post-trains the LLM with DPO across four knowledge-boundary quadrants so the system can abstain with 'I don't know,' evaluated by accuracy plus appropriate abstention. The two works diverge on every coordinate: the problem they treat (corpus-poisoning vulnerability vs. hallucination under knowledge-boundary uncertainty), what they assume about evidence (corpus can be injected with crafted texts vs. retrievals may be noisy/absent), where the change is applied (external knowledge base vs. model weights via preference optimization), what is being scored (ASR for adversarial success vs. honesty-aware QA quality), and the orientation of the work (attack feasibility vs. trustworthiness improvement). There is no shared task, dataset use, or scoring axis that would let one rank or compare them directly.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require both papers to address a common task with a shared evaluation protocol—for example, evaluating DTA's abstention behavior under CPA-RAG-style poisoned corpora on the same datasets, using paired scores such as ASR plus correct-abstention rate. Without overlapping benchmarks, threat models, and unified scoring (e.g., honest-answer rate on clean queries and refusal-or-correctness rate on poisoned queries), the two systems target disjoint problems and cannot be placed on the same leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works pursue opposite goals on different evaluation dimensions: one reports how often crafted documents can flip RAG answers to an adversary-chosen target, while the other reports how well a fine-tuned model balances correct answers with appropriate 'I don't know' responses. Placing their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would invite practitioners to read them as comparable scores when in fact they measure unrelated phenomena, with no shared task, dataset slice, or scoring convention. A reader could easily mistake a high score in one for a stronger system than the other, which would be a serious misreading.

gold_rationale: Paper A studies knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and retrieved context in standard LLMs, proposing a defensive mechanism (PH3) that prunes attention heads to control whether the model favors memory or context, measured by controllability deltas (+44.0% / +38.5%) and open-domain QA. Paper B studies adversarial knowledge poisoning on GraphRAG, proposing two attack algorithms (TKPA, UKPA) operating on the source text used during graph construction, measured by attack success rate (93.1%) and QA degradation (95% to 50%). The failure modes (benign conflict vs. adversarial poisoning), the locus of operation (internal attention heads vs. external corpus text), the metric semantics (defensive control gain vs. offensive degradation), and the stance (mitigation vs. attack) are all incommensurate. Even the evidence assumption differs: Paper A treats both memory and context as potentially correct sources to be balanced, while Paper B treats the corpus as untrusted and manipulable. There is no shared task, model family pipeline (GraphRAG vs. standard RAG/LLM), or benchmark on which a head-to-head numeric comparison would be meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to operate on the same system (e.g., both on GraphRAG or both on standard RAG), share the same threat or task model (both defensive or both offensive, evaluated under a common adversary or conflict generation protocol), use the same QA benchmark with identical retrieval setup and base LLM, and report a commensurable headline number (e.g., post-defense accuracy under poisoning, or attack success rate against a defended system). Ideally one paper's method would be applied as a defense against the other's attack, or both would be evaluated on a shared knowledge-conflict benchmark with matched baselines.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle entirely different problems on different system types: one is about steering an LLM's preference between its own memory and a passage it was given, while the other is about adversaries rewriting source text to corrupt a knowledge graph used by GraphRAG. Their headline numbers describe opposite goals (defending and balancing vs. breaking) on different pipelines and datasets, so placing 44%/38.5% next to 93.1%/50% on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions the experiments do not support.

gold_rationale: The two papers address fundamentally different problems within the RAG umbrella. Paper A (FiD-Light) targets efficiency/latency of generation in an FiD architecture and reports answer-quality plus efficiency metrics under an always-answer policy. Paper B (SURE-RAG) targets evidence sufficiency verification with a three-way SUPPORTED/REFUTED/INSUFFICIENT decision and selective abstention, evaluated by Macro-F1 and risk-at-coverage on HotpotQA-RAG v3 and HaluBench. The failure modes (slow/expensive generation vs. unjustified answers), the evidence treatment (passages consumed by a decoder vs. set-level sufficiency aggregation over a pair verifier), the intervention point (decoder architecture vs. post-retrieval verification layer), the headline metrics (efficiency + QA quality vs. sufficiency Macro-F1 / selective risk), and the answering policy (always answer vs. answer-or-abstain) all diverge. Without a shared task, benchmark, or scoring rule, no leaderboard-style ranking is meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task definition (e.g., open-domain QA with or without abstention), the same benchmark and split, a common evaluation protocol covering both quality and either efficiency or selective-prediction outcomes, and matched retrieval/reader stacks so that one system's contribution can be isolated against the other under identical inputs and scoring.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems are solving different jobs on different datasets with different scoring rules: one is about making retrieval-augmented generation faster while keeping answer quality, the other is about deciding whether retrieved passages actually justify an answer and abstaining when they do not. Putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head winner where none exists, so a practitioner would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is 'better'.

gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets available), Paper A is a 2025 challenge overview report summarizing a community competition on Retrieval-Augmented Generation, while Paper B is a 2019 methodological contribution proposing a specific multi-hop paragraph retrieval algorithm for open-domain QA. The failure_type differs (broad RAG system limitations addressed by many submissions vs. specifically multi-hop reasoning gaps in single-step retrievers). The evidence_assumption differs (LiveRAG's bespoke corpus and questions vs. likely HotpotQA-style benchmarks). The intervention_point differs (a meta-paper aggregating diverse participant approaches vs. one targeted retriever design). The metric_target differs (challenge-specific scoring vs. retrieval precision/recall on multi-hop benchmarks). The action_policy differs (report and synthesize findings across teams vs. recommend a particular retrieval architecture). the two artifacts operate at fundamentally different levels of analysis and on different data.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to evaluate on a shared benchmark with overlapping metrics, address the same retrieval task formulation (e.g., both reporting multi-hop retrieval scores on the same dataset), and present numbers at compatible levels of granularity (system-level method comparison rather than challenge aggregate vs. single method). Additionally, controlling for the six-year gap in foundational models and corpora would be necessary, or restricting the comparison to a clearly delimited subtask where both report comparable numbers.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper summarizes a 2025 community competition that aggregates results across many participating teams on a custom RAG task, while the other is a 2019 paper proposing a specific algorithm for multi-hop paragraph retrieval evaluated on standard QA benchmarks. Placing their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would mislead a practitioner because the two works differ in scope (aggregate report vs. single proposed method), in the underlying datasets, in the era of base models available, and in what counts as a top-line score. A reader could easily draw unsupported conclusions about progress or relative quality.
